error_modes.label: Arrival accuracy in DME at the target fix

texts.0: SP, due to a fix-to-fix solution built on a mis-read present DME, did not arrive at the target fix within the published distance tolerance. The aircraft crossed the fix more than 6 DME off, and the error was still increasing when the IP took the aircraft to re-establish the point-to-point leg. SP did not recognize the divergence from the tuned DME readout at any stage of the transition.
texts.1: SP, due to a single distance solution computed at the start and never revised, did not correct the closure error while the fix-to-fix leg was flown. Arrival distance reached the 4 DME limit of the standard and was reduced only after the IP verbally prompted a recheck of the DME. The correction was applied late and the aircraft stabilized on the fix well after the intended arrival point.
texts.2: SP, due to a coarse first estimate of the distance to run, did not fly the initial transition heading accurately enough to close the fix on the computed profile. Arrival distance opened to about 3 DME from the target fix, between the 2 and 4 DME values of the standard. SP identified the trend on the DME readout in time and closed the error without any IP input.
texts.3: SP computed the distance to the target fix from the DME and flew the transition heading that resolved it. Arrival was inside 2 DME of the fix throughout the leg, with the residual error taken out early and the DME readout used as the primary reference. The solution was reached quickly and without hesitation.
texts.4: SP resolved the fix-to-fix distance problem immediately and flew the leg so that the DME error never exceeded about 1 mile. Arrival over the target fix was essentially exact, with the distance to run reducing at the rate the solution predicted. No re-solution of the problem was required at any point.
texts.marginal: SP arrived at the target fix inside the published distance tolerance, but the DME error sat close to the 2 DME edge of the standard for most of the leg rather than reducing steadily. The trend was toward the outer limit and was arrested only in the last portion of the transition. SP is expected to tighten the running distance check so the arrival error reduces progressively rather than late.

texts_at.1: SP resolved the fix-to-fix distance problem to the standard expected at this stage, letting arrival distance reach the 4 DME limit of the standard before the correction closed the gap. The correction followed the IP's verbal prompt to recheck the DME rather than SP's own running comparison. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to revise the distance solution continuously through the leg rather than computing it once at the start.
texts_at.2: SP identified the trend on the DME readout in time without IP input, letting arrival distance open to about 3 DME from the target fix, between the 2 and 4 DME values of the standard, before closing the error. The first estimate of distance to run is still coarse rather than refined against the running DME. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to refine the first estimate against the DME as soon as the leg begins rather than treating it as fixed.
texts_at.3: SP computed the distance to the target fix from the DME and flew the transition heading that resolved it, arriving inside 2 DME of the fix on most of the leg with the residual error taken out early. One update lagged briefly behind the changing geometry, without the arrival error leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to keep that update as current as the rest of the leg.

texts_above.2: SP identified the trend on the DME readout in time without IP input, letting arrival distance open to about 3 DME from the target fix before closing the error. Refining the first estimate against the DME as soon as the leg begins, rather than treating it as fixed, would keep that opening smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good running-fix discipline.
texts_above.3: SP computed the distance to the target fix from the DME and flew the transition heading that resolved it, arriving inside 2 DME of the fix throughout the leg with the residual error taken out early and the solution reached quickly and without hesitation. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good distance-solution technique.
texts_above.4: SP resolved the fix-to-fix distance problem immediately and flew the leg so the DME error never exceeded about 1 mile, with arrival over the target fix essentially exact and the distance to run reducing at the rate the solution predicted. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent problem resolution.

error_modes.label: Arrival accuracy expressed in radials
error_modes.source: specific:The parameter above (distance) can be expressed in radials

texts.0: SP, due to an incorrect identification of the radial through the target fix, did not arrive on the required bearing from the station. The aircraft crossed the fix more than 6 degrees off the target radial, with no trend toward the correct one, and the IP intervened to re-establish the geometry. SP did not use the bearing pointer to detect that the fix was being approached from the wrong side.
texts.1: SP, due to a transition heading held without any reassessment of the radial being crossed, did not correct the angular error as the fix was approached. The arrival radial error reached the 4 degree limit of the standard and was reduced only after verbal prompting from the IP. The aircraft settled on the correct radial after the intended arrival point.
texts.2: SP, due to a rounded estimate of the angular difference between the present position and the target fix, did not fly the transition heading precisely enough to arrive on the required radial. The error grew to about 3 degrees, between the 2 and 4 degree values of the standard, before SP recognized the bearing trend and adjusted heading without IP input. The fix was then crossed on the correct radial.
texts.3: SP identified the radial through the target fix and flew the transition so that the angular error stayed within 2 degrees. The bearing pointer was used continuously to confirm that the aircraft was closing the correct radial. Arrival over the fix was on the required bearing without a late correction.
texts.4: SP resolved the geometry in radials at once and held the arrival bearing to within about 1 degree of the target radial. The bearing pointer tracked to the fix with no correction of consequence required. The angular solution and the distance solution converged on the same arrival point.
texts.marginal: SP arrived on the target radial within the published tolerance, but the angular error stayed near the 2 degree edge of the standard and was corrected in one late step rather than progressively. The bearing pointer was checked at intervals long enough to let the error accumulate. SP is expected to shorten the interval between bearing checks so the radial error is contained earlier in the transition.

texts_at.1: SP resolved the bearing to the target fix to the standard expected at this stage, letting the arrival radial error reach the 4 degree limit of the standard before it was reduced. The reduction followed verbal prompting from the IP rather than SP's own reassessment of the radial being crossed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to reassess the radial being crossed continuously through the leg rather than holding the transition heading unchanged.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the bearing trend and adjusted heading without IP input, letting the error grow to about 3 degrees, between the 2 and 4 degree values of the standard, before the fix was crossed on the correct radial. The angular estimate is still rounded rather than refined from the bearing pointer as the leg progresses. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to refine the angular estimate from the bearing pointer through the leg rather than holding the first estimate.
texts_at.3: SP identified the radial through the target fix and flew the transition so the angular error stayed within 2 degrees on most of the leg, using the bearing pointer continuously to confirm the correct radial was being closed. One check came slightly later than the others, without the error leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to make that check as promptly as the rest of the leg.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the bearing trend and adjusted heading without IP input, letting the error grow to about 3 degrees before the fix was crossed on the correct radial. Refining the angular estimate from the bearing pointer through the leg, rather than holding the first estimate, would keep that growth smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound bearing management.
texts_above.3: SP identified the radial through the target fix and flew the transition so the angular error stayed within 2 degrees, using the bearing pointer continuously to confirm the aircraft was closing the correct radial with arrival on the required bearing free of a late correction. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed radial tracking.
texts_above.4: SP resolved the geometry in radials at once and held the arrival bearing to within about 1 degree of the target radial, with the bearing pointer tracking to the fix and the angular and distance solutions converging on the same arrival point. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional geometric resolution.

error_modes.label: Timeliness of taking the transition heading

texts.0: SP, due to an attempt to complete the whole fix-to-fix computation before making any control input, did not take the transition heading in time. The aircraft continued on the previous heading for a large part of the available distance, so that the computed solution no longer applied when it was finally flown, and the arrival distance error exceeded 4 DME before the IP directed the turn. The point-to-point leg had to be re-planned from a new present position.
texts.1: SP, due to hesitation over which of two candidate headings to fly, did not turn onto the transition heading at the point the solution required. The delay consumed enough of the leg to bring the arrival error to the 4 DME limit of the standard, and the turn was started only after the IP prompted. SP then flew the heading correctly but from a position that no longer supported an accurate arrival.
texts.2: SP, due to a slow first computation of the transition heading, did not begin the turn immediately when the point-to-point was directed. The turn was started several seconds late and the resulting arrival error reached about 3 DME, between the code 3 and code 1 values of the standard. SP recognized the delay, applied a corrected heading in good time and closed the fix without IP input.
texts.3: SP took the transition heading in time, turning onto the computed heading as soon as the point-to-point was directed. The initial solution was produced quickly enough that no distance was wasted on the previous heading. The aircraft was established on the fix-to-fix leg without delay.
texts.4: SP had the transition heading available almost immediately and rolled onto it with no measurable delay. The turn was made at a rate that put the aircraft on the computed track without overshoot. The whole entry to the point-to-point leg was completed as one continuous action.
texts.marginal: SP took the transition heading within an acceptable time, but the turn was consistently started at the late end of what the solution allowed, leaving little margin for later refinement. The delay did not by itself produce a deviation on this sortie. SP is expected to produce the first heading solution faster so the turn begins as the point-to-point is directed.

texts_at.1: SP took the transition heading to the standard expected at this stage, letting the arrival error reach the 4 DME limit of the standard before the delayed turn was flown. The turn followed the IP's prompt rather than SP's own timing. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to produce the first heading solution fast enough that the turn begins as the point-to-point is directed, not after hesitation between two candidates.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the delay and applied a corrected heading in good time without IP input, letting the arrival error reach about 3 DME, between the code 3 and code 1 values of the standard, before closing the fix. The first computation of the transition heading is still slower than the point-to-point call requires. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to compute the first heading fast enough that no distance is wasted on the previous heading.
texts_at.3: SP took the transition heading in time, turning onto the computed heading as soon as the point-to-point was directed, on most of the leg with no distance wasted on the previous heading. One occasion needed a brief extra moment to settle on the heading, without the arrival error leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to settle on that heading as quickly as on the rest of the exercise.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the delay and applied a corrected heading in good time without IP input, letting the arrival error reach about 3 DME before closing the fix. Computing the first heading fast enough that no distance is wasted on the previous heading would keep that error smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid heading-solution speed.
texts_above.3: SP took the transition heading in time, turning onto the computed heading as soon as the point-to-point was directed, with the initial solution produced quickly enough that no distance was wasted on the previous heading. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate transition timing.
texts_above.4: SP had the transition heading available almost immediately and rolled onto it with no measurable delay, with the turn made at a rate that put the aircraft on the computed track without overshoot as one continuous action. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary transition speed.

error_modes.label: Continuous recomputation and timely correction en route

texts.0: SP, due to treating the initial transition heading as fixed for the whole leg, did not calculate the correct heading continuously during the transition. The geometry changed as the aircraft moved, the deviation grew past 4 DME, beyond the outer values of the standard, and the IP had to intervene to re-solve the problem and regain the fix. No intermediate solution was attempted between the start of the leg and the intervention.
texts.1: SP, due to a scan that returned to the navigation display only at long intervals, did not correct the developing deviation in time. The recomputation was made only after the IP pointed out the divergence, and by then the error was at the 4 DME limit of the standard. The corrected heading was accurate but applied too late to restore the planned arrival.
texts.2: SP, due to recomputing the heading in large steps rather than continuously, did not keep the solution matched to the changing geometry throughout the leg. The deviation opened to about 3 DME, between the code 3 and code 1 limits, before the next update was made. SP detected the trend, applied an intermediate correction in good time and arrived without IP input.
texts.3: SP recalculated the required heading continuously as the geometry changed and corrected the small deviations as they appeared. Each update was applied in time, so the error was held inside the code 3 values for the whole transition. No single large correction was needed near the fix.
texts.4: SP updated the fix-to-fix solution smoothly throughout the leg, so that heading changes were small and made before any deviation became visible. The aircraft tracked to the fix as if flown on a single computed course. The arrival required no correction at all in the final portion.
texts.marginal: SP recalculated the heading during the transition and stayed within standards, but the updates came in a few discrete steps and each was applied at the point where the deviation had already become noticeable. The technique worked on this leg and would not have tolerated a shorter distance to run. SP is expected to move to a continuous update of the solution rather than periodic re-solutions.

texts_at.1: SP recomputed the heading to the standard expected at this stage, letting the deviation reach the 4 DME limit of the standard before the update was applied. The update followed the IP pointing out the divergence rather than SP's own scan of the navigation display. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to return to the navigation display at short, regular intervals rather than only when a divergence is already visible.
texts_at.2: SP detected the trend and applied an intermediate correction in good time without IP input, letting the deviation open to about 3 DME, between the code 3 and code 1 limits, before the update closed it. The heading is still recomputed in large steps rather than continuously through the leg. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to move toward continuous recomputation rather than periodic large updates.
texts_at.3: SP recalculated the required heading continuously as the geometry changed and corrected the small deviations as they appeared on most of the leg, holding the error inside the code 3 values with each update applied in time. One update was a little later than the others, without the error leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to keep that update as prompt as the rest of the leg.

texts_above.2: SP detected the trend and applied an intermediate correction in good time without IP input, letting the deviation open to about 3 DME before the update closed it. Moving toward continuous recomputation, rather than periodic large updates, would keep that opening smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady recomputation discipline.
texts_above.3: SP recalculated the required heading continuously as the geometry changed and corrected the small deviations as they appeared, so the error was held inside the code 3 values for the whole transition with no single large correction needed near the fix. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good continuous updating.
texts_above.4: SP updated the fix-to-fix solution smoothly throughout the leg, so heading changes were small and made before any deviation became visible, with the aircraft tracking to the fix as if flown on a single computed course. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior update continuity.

error_modes.label: Knowledge of the standardized fix-to-fix solution method
error_modes.hf_concept: insufficient knowledge of the published procedure

texts.0: SP, due to lack of knowledge of the published procedure for the condition encountered, did not solve the point-to-point problem according to the standardized method of the Techniques and Procedures Manual and AFMAN 11-202 VOL3. The heading produced was not derived from the present position and target fix geometry, the resulting error exceeded 4 DME, beyond the outer values of the standard, and the IP took the aircraft and demonstrated the solution. SP could not state the steps of the method when questioned in flight.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete knowledge of the standardized fix-to-fix sequence, did not apply the steps in the correct order and produced a heading with a systematic error. The deviation reached the 4 DME limit of the standard and was resolved only after the IP talked SP through the method step by step. SP flew the corrected heading accurately once it had been supplied.
texts.2: SP, due to a partially recalled version of the standardized method, did not apply one step of the solution correctly and produced a heading that was close but not exact. The arrival error stayed near 3 DME, between the code 3 and code 1 values of the standard. SP recognized that the geometry did not match the expected picture, reworked the solution correctly and completed the leg without IP input.
texts.3: SP solved the fix-to-fix problem by the standardized method described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual and AFMAN 11-202 VOL3, with the steps applied in the correct order. The heading produced was correct for the geometry and no IP intervention was required. SP was able to state the reasoning behind the solution when asked.
texts.4: SP applied the standardized point-to-point method flawlessly and produced the correct heading without any intermediate working being visible in the flight path. The method was used identically on each repetition, including the case where the fix lay behind the aircraft. SP explained the solution accurately and immediately when questioned.
texts.marginal: SP solved the problem by the standardized method and stayed within the published values, but the working was slow and one step was reconstructed rather than recalled. Knowledge of the method was sufficient for this geometry and would be thin under a shorter distance to run. SP is expected to consolidate the published sequence so the solution is produced without reconstruction.

texts_at.1: SP applied the standardized fix-to-fix method to the standard expected at this stage, letting the deviation reach the 4 DME limit of the standard before it was resolved. The resolution followed the IP talking through the method step by step rather than SP's own recall. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to consolidate the sequence of steps so the whole method can be applied without being talked through it.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the mismatched geometry and reworked the solution correctly without IP input, letting the arrival error stay near 3 DME, between the code 3 and code 1 values of the standard. One step of the standardized method is still applied imprecisely from a partial recall. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to review that one step until it is recalled as reliably as the rest of the method.
texts_at.3: SP solved the fix-to-fix problem by the standardized method described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual and AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 on most of the leg, with the steps applied in the correct order and the heading correct for the geometry. One step was worked out a little more slowly than the others, without an error resulting. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to recall that step as promptly as the rest of the method.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the mismatched geometry and reworked the solution correctly without IP input, letting the arrival error stay near 3 DME. Reviewing the one step still recalled only partially, until it is as reliable as the rest of the method, would remove that mismatch. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured method application.
texts_above.3: SP solved the fix-to-fix problem by the standardized method described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual and AFMAN 11-202 VOL3, with the steps applied in the correct order and no IP intervention required, stating the reasoning behind the solution when asked. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise procedural recall.
texts_above.4: SP applied the standardized point-to-point method flawlessly and produced the correct heading without any intermediate working visible in the flight path, using the method identically on every repetition including the case where the fix lay behind the aircraft. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate method fluency.

error_modes.label: Wind and groundspeed accounting on the point-to-point leg

texts.0: SP, due to a solution computed without any allowance for the known wind, did not correct the drift that developed along the fix-to-fix leg. The aircraft was displaced progressively downwind, the arrival error exceeded 4 DME and 4 degrees, beyond the outer values of the standard in both distance and radial, and the IP intervened to re-establish the track. SP did not compare the actual bearing trend with the trend the no-wind solution predicted.
texts.1: SP, due to a drift correction estimated once and never revised against the observed bearing change, did not keep the aircraft on the computed track. The displacement built up to the 4 DME and 4 degree limits of the standard and was corrected only after the IP called attention to the bearing pointer. The final part of the leg was flown with a large drift correction that had to be removed again near the fix.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial drift allowance that was smaller than the actual wind required, did not hold the computed track through the first part of the transition. The error opened to about 3 DME and 3 degrees, between the code 3 and code 1 limits, before SP compared the observed and expected bearing rates. The drift correction was then increased in good time and the fix was made without IP input.
texts.3: SP allowed for the wind in the transition heading and adjusted the drift correction as the observed bearing rate indicated. The aircraft held the computed track and arrived at the fix inside the code 3 values in both distance and radial. Groundspeed was used to confirm the time and distance to run.
texts.4: SP incorporated the wind into the solution from the outset and refined the drift correction by very small amounts as the bearing rate confirmed it. The track to the fix stayed effectively straight and the arrival error was negligible. Groundspeed and distance to run agreed throughout the leg.
texts.marginal: SP allowed for drift and remained within the published values, but the correction was set from the forecast wind and adjusted only once against what the instruments showed. The residual displacement stayed near the edge of the code 3 band for part of the leg. SP is expected to derive the drift correction from the observed bearing rate rather than relying on the pre-flight wind.

texts_at.1: SP allowed for wind on the fix-to-fix leg to the standard expected at this stage, letting the displacement build to the 4 DME and 4 degree limits before the correction was applied. The correction followed the IP calling attention to the bearing pointer rather than SP's own comparison of the bearing trend. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to revise the drift correction against the observed bearing change rather than estimating it once at the start.
texts_at.2: SP compared the observed and expected bearing rates without IP input, letting the error open to about 3 DME and 3 degrees, between the code 3 and code 1 limits, before increasing the drift correction in good time. The initial drift allowance is still smaller than the wind actually requires. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to size the initial allowance from the observed wind rather than a smaller planning figure.
texts_at.3: SP allowed for the wind in the transition heading and adjusted the drift correction as the observed bearing rate indicated on most of the leg, holding the computed track and arriving inside the code 3 values in both distance and radial. One adjustment came slightly later than the rest, without the arrival error leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to make that adjustment as promptly as the rest of the leg.

texts_above.2: SP compared the observed and expected bearing rates without IP input, letting the error open to about 3 DME and 3 degrees before increasing the drift correction in good time. Sizing the initial allowance from the observed wind, rather than a smaller planning figure, would keep that opening smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable drift-rate comparison.
texts_above.3: SP allowed for the wind in the transition heading and adjusted the drift correction as the observed bearing rate indicated, holding the computed track and arriving at the fix inside the code 3 values in both distance and radial with groundspeed used to confirm time and distance to run. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good wind accounting.
texts_above.4: SP incorporated the wind into the solution from the outset and refined the drift correction by very small amounts as the bearing rate confirmed it, with the track to the fix staying effectively straight and the arrival error negligible. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior drift refinement.

error_modes.label: Instrument cross-check and aircraft control while solving the problem

texts.0: SP, due to an attention bottleneck on the navigation display at the expense of the instrument cross-check, did not maintain the aircraft state while working the point-to-point problem. Attitude, altitude and heading were left unmonitored long enough for the flight path to diverge, and the arrival error passed 4 DME before the IP took the aircraft. The navigation solution was also not completed, so both the flying and the problem were lost together.
texts.1: SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check while attention remained on the fix-to-fix computation, did not keep the primary flight parameters under control during the transition. The deviation reached the 4 DME limit of the standard and was recovered only after the IP called for a return to the basic scan. SP then flew the aircraft accurately but had to restart the navigation solution.
texts.2: SP, due to a scan that dwelt on the navigation display while the problem was being worked, did not cross-check the primary flight instruments at the required rate. Heading and altitude drifted enough to place the arrival error near 3 DME, between the code 3 and code 1 values of the standard. SP recognized the narrowed scan, re-established the cross-check and corrected the deviation without IP input.
texts.3: SP kept the instrument cross-check running while solving the point-to-point problem, so that attitude, altitude and heading were held throughout the transition. The navigation work was fitted into the scan rather than replacing it. The fix was made inside the code 3 values with the aircraft state stable.
texts.4: SP worked the fix-to-fix solution without any detectable interruption of the instrument cross-check. The primary flight parameters were held essentially constant while the heading updates were computed and applied. Aircraft control and navigation were carried out as a single integrated task.
texts.marginal: SP kept the aircraft within standards while solving the problem, but the cross-check narrowed toward the navigation display each time a new heading was computed, and the primary parameters moved slightly before being recaptured. Capacity was adequate for this workload and left little margin for an added task. SP is expected to keep the basic scan running continuously while the point-to-point solution is worked.

texts_at.1: SP kept the aircraft state under control while solving the problem to the standard expected at this stage, letting the deviation reach the 4 DME limit of the standard before it was recovered. The recovery followed the IP calling for a return to the basic scan rather than SP's own cross-check. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to keep the primary flight instruments in the scan while the fix-to-fix computation is worked, not set them aside for it.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the narrowed scan and re-established the cross-check without IP input, letting the arrival error near 3 DME, between the code 3 and code 1 values of the standard, before the deviation was corrected. The scan is still dwelling on the navigation display while the problem is being worked rather than moving between the two tasks. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to fit the navigation work into the cross-check rather than letting the scan dwell on it.
texts_at.3: SP kept the instrument cross-check running while solving the point-to-point problem on most of the transition, so attitude, altitude and heading were held with the fix made inside the code 3 values. One stretch showed a brief narrowing of the scan during the busiest part of the computation, without a deviation resulting. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to keep the scan as wide through that stretch as through the rest of the transition.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the narrowed scan and re-established the cross-check without IP input, letting the arrival error near 3 DME before the deviation was corrected. Fitting the navigation work into the cross-check, rather than letting the scan dwell on it, would keep that error smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent scan integration.
texts_above.3: SP kept the instrument cross-check running while solving the point-to-point problem, so attitude, altitude and heading were held throughout the transition with the navigation work fitted into the scan rather than replacing it and the fix made inside the code 3 values. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined workload sharing.
texts_above.4: SP worked the fix-to-fix solution without any detectable interruption of the instrument cross-check, holding the primary flight parameters essentially constant while the heading updates were computed and applied, with aircraft control and navigation carried out as a single integrated task. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless task integration.

error_modes.label: GPS/RNAV direct-to-fix setup and mode management

texts.0: SP, due to mode confusion over the selected navigation source and what it was displaying, did not set up the direct-to-fix navigation correctly for the assigned point. The aircraft was flown toward a waypoint other than the one required and the resulting error passed 4 DME, far outside the published values, before the IP intervened and reselected the correct fix. SP did not cross-check the GPS/RNAV picture against the VOR/DME or TACAN raw data at any stage.
texts.1: SP, due to acceptance of the automated solution without an independent check of the parameters, did not verify that the direct-to entry matched the fix that had been assigned. The discrepancy was identified only after the IP questioned the displayed track, by which time the error was at the 4 DME limit of the standard. SP corrected the entry and flew the leg accurately from that point.
texts.2: SP, due to a slow and partly incorrect sequence in entering the direct-to fix, did not complete the RNAV setup before the transition heading was required. The first part of the leg was flown on an approximate heading and the arrival error stayed near 3 DME, between the code 3 and code 1 values. SP completed the entry, cross-checked it against the raw data and refined the heading without IP input.
texts.3: SP set up the direct-to-fix navigation for the assigned point correctly and confirmed it against the VOR/DME or TACAN raw data before turning. The selected mode and the displayed track were identified before they were used to fly the aircraft. The fix was made inside the code 3 values of the standard.
texts.4: SP configured the RNAV direct-to fix immediately and verified the entry, the active mode and the raw-data picture as one check. The transition heading was flown from a solution that the GPS and the ground-based aids both supported. No reselection or re-entry was needed at any point in the leg.
texts.marginal: SP set up the direct-to-fix navigation correctly and remained within the published values, but the entry was verified against the raw data only after the turn had been started. The cross-check confirmed rather than preceded the action. SP is expected to confirm the selected fix and mode against the raw data before flying the computed heading.

texts_at.1: SP set up direct-to-fix navigation to the standard expected at this stage, letting the error reach the 4 DME limit of the standard before the entry was corrected. The distance error passed 4 DME and the IP took over the navigation to re-establish the leg.

texts.2: SP, due to a momentary reversal of the tail of the bearing pointer and the head of the course arrow when building the EHSI picture, did not select the correct side of the geometry on the first attempt. texts.3: SP identified the present position between the tail of the bearing pointer and the centre of the EHSI, and the target fix between the centre and the head of the course arrow, before selecting any heading. texts.4: SP read the EHSI picture without hesitation, placing present position and target fix on their correct sides of the display each time the geometry was reassessed. texts.marginal: SP placed the present position and the target fix correctly on the EHSI, but needed a second look at the tail of the bearing pointer before committing to a heading on more than one update.
